Posted April 10, 2003
Special Report to MarijuanaNews.com by Richard Cowan

The Kubby refugee hearings resumed today in Vancouver with some truly damning testimony about the sad state of the DEAland justice system from people who are in a position to know the truth all too well.
See
 As Kubby Refugee Hearings Resume. Government Makes Its Case Clear, If Not Well. And I Have Lunch With A Prohibitionist. Special Report to MarijuanaNews.com

The first witness by phone was Angel McClary Raich, a patient/activist who was also a medical necessity plaintiff in the Oakland CBC case that sought unsuccessfully to get the Supreme Court to allow the Oakland club to distribute cannabis to people whose lives depend upon it.
See
 The Ultimate Hypocrisy: " Justice " Thomas, Who Smoked Marijuana At Yale Law School, Writes Supreme Court Opinion Against Medical Cannabis. Drug War Depends Upon Persecution of Sick and Dying.

She is also suing to try to get the Federal courts to enjoin the DEA from arresting patients. Last month, the local federal court declined to act on her suit, so she is appealing. The point is that the Feds refuse to recognize that there is any such thing as medical cannabis, despite state laws. (Her husband, attorney Robert Raich, is handling the suit and is also an attorney for the Oakland club. Both are very dear friends, so I am even less dispassionate than usual about this case.)

Angel has a variety of life-threatening diseases that cause her constant pain and nausea, which only cannabis alleviates. She testified about how she was shocked when it was first suggested to her that cannabis might help, and how she became an activist to try to help others when she learned the truth.

Even though she is very petite, she needs a very large quantity of cannabis, which is grown for her by two friends who were also plaintiffs in seeking the injunction. Understandably, they are listed as John Doe #1, and John Doe #2.

Angel described having to live in fear of being arrested, or having one of her growers arrested. The number of plants required for her would result in their facing very long Federal mandatory minimums, plus conspiracy charges. Such an ordeal would undoubtedly prove fatal long before she ever got to trial. It would be a torturous death for me, she said.

Gordon Starr, the lawyer for the Canadian Immigration Minister, whose job it is to fight the refugee claims by Kubby, Tuck and Hayes, tried to lead her testimony in such a way as to imply that it would be safe for the Kubbys to return to California. After all, Angel has been very outspoken and she has not been arrested yet. So surely, Steve Kubby could go back and grow his own medicine and not have any problems from the Feds.

However, Angel pointed out that the Feds have raided patients with as few as six plants. She also talked about a number of other raids on patients immediately after 9/11. It was quite clear from her testimony that she does not feel safe.

In fact, she described the toll that the stress has already taken on her health. Angel is an enormously effective witness, and I have no doubt that the Adjudicator and the Refugee Protection officer, both female, were deeply moved by her testimony about her children.

While Angel put the human face on the plight of the patients, California Judge James Gray of the Orange County Superior Court painted a frightening picture of the DEAland criminal justice system.

Gray is a former Federal prosecutor, who is now strongly opposed to the Drug War. He is the perfect witness, in that he is a law and order conservative, appointed by a Republican governor, and he doesn't even drink. He also complained that the Drug War has swamped the court system and filled our prisons. He talked about the prison/industrial complex and how the Drug War has become a huge industry that depends on keeping cannabis illegal. In one of the better descriptions of prohibition, he called it unworkable, but imminently fundable.

Gray said that he doubted that Kubby could be convicted in a California state court, although he could still be arrested, but the greatest danger would come from the Feds. In fact, his comments on the Federal government's behavior probably shocked the Canadians.

He even called John Ashcroft's position on medical cannabis extremist. He added, What I've seen here in the federal government is appalling. He added that Kubby would face what amounted to cruel and unusual punishment.

He said that there is a Drug War exception to the Bill of Rights. There are no states rights and no 9th and 10th Amendments, but Where is our Paul Revere?

What utterly damning comments from a conservative sitting judge!

Ironically, while Gray was testifying, the Congress was making matters even worse by eliminating what little discretion that Federal judges have about imposing mandatory minimums in drug cases.

Amazingly, this outrageous act was taken without any debate in the Senate because it was attached to the so-called Amber Alert bill, providing Federal funding for a system to track kidnap victims. This allows them to pretend to be concerned about children.

However, his closing comments were even more devastating. Judge Gray said that if someone near and dear to me were in Steve Kubby's position, I would strongly advise him not to return to America. He even told the Adjudicator, If it were your brother, it would be a risk not to be taken.

The final witness was Ed Rosenthal who reiterated what Gray and Raich had said, and went into detail about how juries in Federal courts are blocked from hearing any reference to medical cannabis, or the defendant's medical condition.
See
 Astonishing Editorial In New York Times Attacks Rosenthal Prosecution. Finally Taking The Issue Seriously?

Tomorrow, Placer County DA Chris Cattran will testify, but it was clear from today's testimony that state laws are irrelevant. The refugees are here because they cannot get a fair trial in DEAland. That should qualify them for refugee status under Canadian law.

The problem for Canada is that they understandably want to avoid saying that DEAland is DEAland. They are wasting a lot of money on these hearings, and should just pull the plug on the process and stop trying to send people to their deaths in a country that even conservative judges call appalling in its treatment of the sick and dying.

It was a good day for my friends, an awkward day for Canada, and a very sad day for the land of the free and the home of the brave.
